speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, I request the unanimous consent of the House to present a motion dealing with an important and urgent matter.
In view of the gravity of the consequences of the conflict generated by the air controllers and pilots of Canada, except for the Gens de l'air du Quebec, as the protocol of agreement signed by CALPA, CATCA and the Minister of Transport constitutes one of the worst affronts ever inflicted upon the government in the history of this country, as the decision of the Minister of Transport is stamped with chauvinism and racism which are contrary to the most elementary rights of the francophone citizens in Canada, and taking into account the fact that all the right-minded hon. members of this Parliament cannot associate themselves with so revolting an act, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette):
That this House demand immediately that a recorded vote be taken so that all Canadians might know who, in this House, disapprove or approve of the attitude of the Minister of Transport in the conflict that opposes him to the air controllers and pilots in Canada, a positive vote leading necessarily to the resignation of the minister concerned.

loss of revenue which the provinces will suffer as a result of the government's announced intention to terminate the revenue guarantee payments, will the minister tell the House whether the government is considering the transfer of tax points to compensate the provinces for these losses, and further, given that the federal government has unilaterally changed the formula for the revenue guarantee payments owing for fiscal years already completed thus breaking an existing agreement with the provinces, will the government reconsider this decision so as to restore an atmosphere of basic trust to the current negotiations?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should point out to the hon. lady-

speechtext:
-that the arrangements for the revenue guarantee were with regard to a five year period which would enable the provinces to adjust their own taxation systems to the changes brought about by the tax reform. We have made it clear to the provinces that we do not intend to continue beyond 1976 the sweeping revenue guarantee that has existed in the past, and of course it was understood that the provinces over the intervening five years would have to adjust their own taxation systems to take care of the change in revenue that would be brought about.
The hon. lady refers to our claim back for the years that are now closed, 1972 and 1973. It is true that there was a federal over-payment by about $300 million in respect of those two fiscal years. We have made it clear, both in the House and to the provinces, that we are not seeking to claim back that amount for those years.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Finance. As federal revenues since tax reform have exceeded expectations, and as the minister has made this point quite clear in giving reasons why the provincial revenue guarantees should be terminated retroactively, does the minister propose, now that revenue guarantee payments will likely no longer take place, the reduction of federal tax rates so that the excess revenue referred to by the minister and others may lessen and so that the Canadian taxpayer will not be double taxed as a result of the federal action? Let us remember that there is only one taxpayer for all levels of government.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF TAX REDUCTION IN VIEW OF EXCESS REVENUES
speechtext: Exactly, Mr. Speaker, and that is why I point out to the hon. gentleman, as I pointed out to the provinces, that there was no excess revenue coming to the government of Canada, but if, as the provinces insisted, the full amount of the revenue guarantee, as calculated by the econometric formula, be paid to the provinces, then there would have to be an increase in federal taxation against federal taxpayers for the purpose of paying that greater amount. We feel that the provinces have been indemnified for what they have expected, as indicated in their own budgetary statements, and that they should not be claiming something greater than indemnity.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I, too, have a question with regard to the cost-sharing proposals of the federal government. By giving the provinces, as a substitute for the present 50-50 cost-sharing on health and post-secondary education, a new package which is substantially dependent on tax points, I would like to ask the minister whether he agrees that this leaves the provinces much more vulnerable in these precise areas in the sense that provincial taxes for almost all provinces are levied as a percentage of the federal tax, and therefore if the federal government changes its tax policy, the provinces could well get less revenue than they had planned for, as happened when the government introduced indexing.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance
subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS EFFECT ON PROVINCIAL REVENUES OF TRANSFER OF TAX POINTS TO REPLACE COST-SHARING PROGRAMS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should correct the hon. gentleman. The proposal is not principally on tax points. On the several options mentioned, one provides for a 66% per cent payment in cash, another for 50 per cent in cash, with the balance for transmittal in terms of tax points. The basic proposition the hon. gentleman puts with respect to the impact on the provincial tax base on personal income tax is quite correct. I would remind him, however, that at least from some of the provinces-and there was evidence of this again at the meeting yesterday-there has been insistence on the transfer of tax points because they know that in the long run these taxes will return them a far greater yield than would cash payments.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS EFFECT ON PROVINCIAL REVENUES OF TRANSFER OF TAX POINTS TO REPLACE COST-SHARING PROGRAMS
speechtext: To be perfectly clear then, the minister is conceding that by shifting away from a 50-50 cost-sharing formula in relation to health care and post-secondary education costs to a system which weighs heavily-I shall not put it more strongly than that-on the tax point system, leaves the provinces in a much more vulnerable position in terms of ability to forecast their own revenue expectations to cover the fields I have mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS EFFECT ON PROVINCIAL REVENUES OF TRANSFER OF TAX POINTS TO REPLACE COST-SHARING PROGRAMS

This, presumably, was well known to those provinces which sought not only half the transfer but the whole of the transfer of tax points. So, now it looks like it depends very much on where you sit in this country. With regard to the less well-favoured provinces, the cash payment has more effect than the transfer of tax points.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of Finance. As investment by Canadian businessmen in foreign countries during the past five years has tripled-in 1975 it exceeded foreign investment in Canada by $200 million-is the minister considering plans to make investment in Canada at least as attractive as investment abroad with consequence advantages to Canadian production and employment? If that is the case, would the minister announce what these plans are at the first opportunity on motions?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance

I am
not proposing at this point to make any statement on further fiscal changes of the kind set out by my predeces-

sor to stimulate manufacturing and processing investment in Canada. In my view, the principal concern investors might have felt with respect to Canada was the rate of inflation in this country, together with the rate of increase in cost due to high wage settlements. As the hon. member knows, we have set ourselves, under the anti-inflation policy, the goal of reducing the rate of inflation and, as a consequence, reducing the increase in industrial costs, perhaps the most important single factor in reaching investment decisions.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO MAKE INVESTMENT IN CANADA MORE ATTRACTIVE TO CANADIANS
speechtext: Considering the government's obvious lack of intent to make investment in this country more attractive for Canadian businessmen, is it any wonder Canadian businessmen are forced to make large investments abroad, as they are presently doing?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO MAKE INVESTMENT IN CANADA MORE ATTRACTIVE TO CANADIANS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would have to say to the hon. member, and to those in the business community who share his thinking, that the primary goal in Canada for all Canadians should be the overcoming of inflation in this country.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO MAKE INVESTMENT IN CANADA MORE ATTRACTIVE TO CANADIANS
speechtext: What about overcoming unemployment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO MAKE INVESTMENT IN CANADA MORE ATTRACTIVE TO CANADIANS
speechtext: This is always a critical factor. I point out to the hon. gentleman that if we fail to overcome inflation the rate of unemployment will be very much greater in Canada. As for those people who state they would not enter into investments for plant and equipment which would have a useful life of between 20 and 25 years because of the interim nature of the anti-inflation program, I suggest to them that they should do their thinking again. We believe that Canada is and will be a good investment area for Canadian and foreign business, and that they have as much to gain as any of us by supporting the anti-inflation program; and the attitudes of some members of the business community which negate the anti-inflation program really are negating their own interests as well.

speechtext: The House resumed, from Tuesday, July 6, 1976, consideration of Bill C-84, to amend the Criminal Code in relation to the punishment for murder and certain other serious offences, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, and motion No. 13 (Mr. Reynolds).

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the close of our sitting last evening I was speaking on this amendment which calls for the deletion of section 214 of the Criminal Code dealing particularly with the substitution of life imprisonment for first-degree murder, which would mean a period of 25 years in the case of a person convicted of the murder of a police officer, a prison guard

or a correctional officer. As I said, I support the amendment because if this clause were deleted we would go back to the law as it was.
I pointed out last evening that an undertaking was given by the government 2Vi years ago. It was a promise, a commitment to the House, to parliament and to the country that if parliament would buy the government's part retention and part abolition bill, that would be the policy. Notwithstanding the commitment that was made, that commitment and promise has not been kept and here we are, 2Vi years later, again arguing the same question.
Because I support this amendment I have a few statistics I should like to place on the record. The number of prison guards killed since 1961 totals six. The number of persons who were convicted and sentenced for a first murder, subsequently jailed and who committed a second murder in Canada in the last 10 or 15 years, is five. The number of policemen killed on duty since 1961 is 57. The number of custodial officers murdered since 1961 is six. Yet we have heard the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) at the committee level and in this House on occasion deny that there are any records of second murders.
What protection do the guards and the correctional officers have when, as I pointed out last night and the Solicitor General admitted at the committee level, these people, given a sentence of 25 years, may, with an escort, be released from prison at any time? What is to stop the guard and the escort being knocked off? We had a case of a person being escorted from one jail to another who asked to go to the bathroom, where he obtained a gun and then killed the police officer when he was being escorted from one institution to another. I support this amendment because I think it is very important.
The last thought I would leave is that I am shocked to think of the situation in which we are placing police officers, guards and correctional officers. I pointed out the number who have lost their lives, without adequate compensation for their families who suffer because of either the first or second murder these people commit. I ask the Solicitor General, if this bill should pass on third reading, to conduct an honest and responsible review in an effort to see that the families of the police officers, guards and correctional officers, who are victims, are compensated for the death of the provider.
Surely it is not too much to ask that greater attention be paid to victims rather than to the accused, contrary to what those liberals, with a small "1", wish, which is to change the law and always favour the accused rather than the victim. I have only spoken once in this debate and once on the amendments, and I leave that thought, through you, Mr. Speaker, with the Solicitor General. I am not talking about compensation amounting only to peanuts. I am talking about compensation which would really compensate the family of the victim whose life was lost violently at the hands of people released from prison who commit murder for the second time under the law as it exists now and as it may exist if this bill is given third reading and passed.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words to support the motion before us. Recently I had the opportunity to meet a convict who was on parole. Of course the capital punishment issue was raised and I wish to tell you the essence of what this man told me: He said: I favour the amendment to the Criminal Code. I think it amounts to abolishing capital punishment. Bill C-84 proposes to abolish capital punishment and replace it by a period of imprisonment for 25 years. If I am given the choice between capital punishment and 25 years in jail, I shall choose jail in the hope of escaping. Then he told me that his trade was theft, armed robbery and that over a few years he had committed several thefts in different areas of the country and made more than $1 million. He added: I enjoy a certain legal immunity following a court judgment exonerating me of all blame for my involvement in those crimes. You will readily understand, he said, that I am for the abolition of capital punishment and for firearms control as family men and other businessmen will no longer be allowed to have firearms. They will not be able to defend themselves against us who will continue to use firearms. Of course the legislation will not say explicitly that murderers can keep their weapons notwithstanding the regulations, but it is implied as our trade requires the uncontrolled possession of firearms.
This is why syndicates of professional killers exert pressure on hon. members for the abolition of capital punishment. You will also understand, he added, that the people in our trade must be free to operate without the threat of capital punishment.
And we must of necessity have firearms, and also some kind of protection, assurances against those who would not let us take their property or their lives. Contract killers have a right to earn a living without hindrance, don't they, Mr. Solicitor General? I see he is absent for the moment.
Killers and thieves are supported by revolutionaries and outlaws, who also require guns. Once firearms have been controlled and capital punishment abolished by Parliament, killers and thieves of all kinds finally will be able to breathe. In countries where firearms are controlled and capital punishment abolished, professional criminals are quite prosperous. They enjoy complete safety. That is why professional criminals spare neither efforts nor money to ensure speedy passing of firearms control and abolition.
Firearms control and abolition go hand in hand. Through abolition, routine perpetration of theft and murder will become easier. That is what the government can expect if this legislation goes through. Mr. Speaker, certainly it is only human that people get emotional during a murder trial. The majority of people tend to react violently when a criminal gets a sentence out of keeping with what the community expects. Recently the Solicitor General, the

Capital Punishment
Hon. Warren Allmand, went on record to state he would not want at any price to be associated in any way with a hanging. This was a debasing act, he said, which did not solve in any way the problem of crime in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, while agreeing that the reinstatement of capital punishment will not solve every crime problem in Canada, the question we must address ourselves is this: Will reinstatement in effect solve the problem for some? Indeed, Mr. Speaker, some time ago in Oshawa, a young man shot his parents and then gave himself up to the police, but he was still holding his loaded gun and was ready to fire at the slightest movement of the policeman who arrested him. During the interrogation he was asked: Why did you not shoot the policeman? He answered quite frankly that he simply did not want to be hanged.
Personally, I am satisfied that on various occasions several police officers or prison guards were saved because, in principle, the death penalty is applied for the murder of a police officer or a prison guard; I think that is the reason. If we could better plan the operations of our rehabilitation institutions and of our penitentiaries, perhaps we could improve and correct several imperfections or problems. Of course, Mr. Speaker, when the Solicitor General of Canada, the hon. Warren Allmand, presented this bill, he was not the only one to support that opinion, quite the contrary.
He feels supported by the whole cabinet and by a good majority of the Liberal caucus. He is more strongly supported by his colleagues than by the Canadian population. As a member of the Canadian Parliament, in all justice, I think that it is undeniable that the present government should take into account that 81 per cent of the Canadian population is in favour of maintaining the death penalty.
The Solicitor General of Canada says that the death penalty will not act as a deterrent for potential murderers. This may be true to a certain extent. But long prison terms will have very little deterring effect, and this logic were carried to extremes, one would have to conclude that criminals should be rewarded.
Mr. Speaker, we all know that many crimes are not premeditated and that those responsible are not hanged for such offences. We, of the Social Credit Party of Canada, want the death penalty to be applied only in cases where premeditation is clearly established. Moreover, the Solicitor General claims that the death penalty does not reduce at all the number of murders in Canada. In this regard, let me point out that since 1962, when the last hanging took place in Canada, murders have increased by 42 per cent, or 1.7 per cent per 100,000 inhabitants and 2.4 per cent for the total population.
In my humble opinion, Mr. Speaker, by voting for Bill C-84, the members and ministers of this illustrious assembly are giving future murderers who are condemned to life imprisonment a free hand to kill all those who stand between them and freedom. Under this bill, someone facing life imprisonment, either for armed robbery or for any other crime liable to this sentence, would actually benefit from killing the incriminating witness or witnesses or the policeman. This action would have the advantage of enabling him to escape without any risk of increasing the sentence he must serve. The myth that a murderer rarely repeats his crime may be true when the murder is commit-

ted on the spur of the moment, but it is something else when a murder is committed by a professional killer.
If the death penalty were maintained, those would be the ones to be punished and they would deserve it. Moreover, the Solicitor General claims that murderers should not suffer the death penalty. But what alternative solution does he propose? That policemen and prison guards be better trained? Is the Solicitor General of Canada suggesting that all the policemen or prison guards who died on duty were not well trained? To this, I would reply that in most large cities such as Detroit and Montreal policemen are very well trained and armed, but violence is on the increase in these cities.
Moreover an effective gun control system, such as that proposed in Bill C-83, does not give more protection. On the contrary, its sole effect is to restrict the freedom and the rights of honest people. I really believe that the present legislation should be applied more severely to criminals and outlaws. Gun control might reduce certain types of violence, but in my humble opinion, it will have no effect on cold-blooded killers. Our social and economic security programs no longer truly meet present needs. A proof of this is that in the last few years, crime has been increasing. I believe we should review our way of life and take action to ensure that authority at all levels is respected, and to that end, we should start by applying the death penalty in Canada to people convicted of premeditated murder.

Mr. Speaker, this issue demands our calm reflection. First, let it be said that when the people of a nation make their position on any issue known, there is some kind of emotional underpinning to their position. When it is said that 80 per cent of Canadians favour capital punishment, I think it can be said, equally validly, that most people are not asking for the imposition of capital punishment per se but are saying that they have lost faith in the law and order system of this country.
Consequently, since Canadians across this country have lost faith in our ability to maintain law and order and ask for capital punishment, we are brought face to face with the fact that the government has done nothing to make people feel that if capital punishment is removed from the statute books, they will be secure.
What do the people of this country face? On the one hand they face the prospect of the abolition of the death penalty; on the other hand there is no indication of any identifiable concern with regard to the increasing incidence of violent crime in this country.
The government introduced Bill C-84 as a companion bill to Bill C-83 which was to extend protection to Canadians. It is well known that Canadians do not think Bill C-83 will ensure a greater measure of public security and safety. The amendment proposed by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds) would reinstitute that which the government reneged on during two five-year experimental periods, namely, capital punishment for the murderers of police officers and those engaged in security and guarding roles.
July 7, 1976

If we consider the situation which faces the people of this country, we must recognize that even if this bill passes there will still be a continuance in this country of a form of capital punishment. Therefore, the fundamental question we face is whether there is to be a trial before the imposition of capital punishment. This question becomes obvious when one considers the unfortunate position in which we may place our police officers. As it is, the government has done little to improve our security and decrease violent crime in this country. It has done nothing to lessen the psychology of crime heightened by television and the movies. It has done nothing with regard to child-abuse laws, and has done little to negate impressions created by the press in sensationalizing crime. Because of lack of government action, if the capital punishment sanction is removed from the statute books we shall live in a law and order vacuum, as I shall soon demonstrate.
Consider how police officers will act. Because they will not be protected, we can expect that policemen, faced with people of intemperate or violent temper, will shoot first and ask questions afterwards. Therefore, even under the new regime of Bill C-84 we shall have a continuation of capital punishment but it will be capital punishment without trial. If we look at the question calmly, we will realize that we are not debating whether or not there is to be capital punishment in this country: we are debating whether or not there is to be a trial, whether we are to continue to extend to people the right to a fair hearing before sentence is imposed. If you weaken the protection afforded to the police forces of this country, it goes without saying that when policemen act under duress, people will be killed. Policemen will obviously want to feel secure and, not having the protection of the law, will shoot first and ask questions afterwards.
The real question at issue is not whether we are to be an abolitionist or retentionist state. The real issue is whether the government has taken the necessary measures to protect us all by way of law and order, has taken those measures which are the prerequisite of abolition of capital punishment. How can you remove the sanction of capital punishment unless you have first removed the threat of violent crime in this country? But the fact is that violent crime in the last ten years has increased over 300 per cent-and violent crimes are reported daily in the press and on radio and television.
I do not argue that Canada should never be an abolitionist state, but I do say that the government could explore at least 50 different avenues for making the social environment of the citizens of this country safer and reducing the incidence of violent crime. Only after crime has been reduced can we become an abolitionist state. If we now remove the death penalty we shall threaten the safety of policemen and cause them to use their weapons more readily in order to protect their own lives. That brings us back to the fundamental question I first raised: Even if this bill passes, we shall continue to have capital punishment, but this time without trial.
The amendment put forward by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta does not ask whether we have capital punishment; it asks whether we have due process of law. That is something very fundamental that we should
Capital Punishment
be exercising and talking about at this time. If the government wants to take the position of being an abolitionist state, it must first demonstrate clearly to Canadians that they come first and that law and order against violent crime is intact. What is important is not the question of whether we are abolitionist or retentionist, but whether the people of Canada are being protected. According to statistics, about 80 per cent of Canadians are in favour of retention. That is a reflection of the mood of Canadians about law and order, more than a reflection of their mood about hanging or the death penalty.
According to a survey which I conducted in my constituency, 86.6 per cent are in favour of capital punishment. What is really symbolic is that these Canadians have lost faith in the fact that they are secure in this country. It does not necessarily imply that they want people to be hung or executed in some other form, but that before we disband capital punishment, whatever needs to be done ought to be done. The government must earn the right to be an abolitionist state. They must have a valid reason for taking away the death penalty.
The government has twice brought forward an experiment in five years with capital punishment only for those people who have killed a police officer or a security guard. However, that is a period that has never been honoured. Something which disturbs Canadians very much is that they are being asked to accept a change in law with regard to capital punishment when they note very clearly that for a period of nearly a decade the government has not obeyed its own law. If we are to believe in law, if it is to be a fundamental cornerstone of our democratic society, then surely the government must obey and practice the laws that it puts on the statute books. The fact that the government has ignored its own laws and regulations certainly enhances the distrust of Canadians.
I do not believe in the concept of "an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth." That does not underscore any purpose. We would have a whole nation that is blind and toothless. Those who believe in the notion of an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth are really saying, "Do not get angry; get even." We must have a feeling that has some purpose. At the present time there is an eroding of the feeling of security and law and order. Without the protection of the death sentence for those who will kill for the second time in order to escape from an institution, once having been incarcerated for a crime of murder, police and prison guards are in the vulnerable position of having to protect themselves in the psychology of "shoot first and ask questions later." We must underscore the fact that the government needs to earn the right to implement an abolitionist state. We must also recognize the fear that our police officers and prison guards will have.
If this amendment is not passed, capital punishment will not be done away with. It will be simply a case of the due course of law not being followed. Police officers and prison guards in this country will, in more rapid succession, be using their weapons in self-defence. The result will be capital punishment without trial.
The government has an obligation to ensure that we retain intact the symbol of peace and security. In my second reading speech I listed in some detail a number of different aspects that would assist our achieving a situa-

July 7, 1976
Capital Punishment
tion of peace and security. It is extremely important that we begin to move toward a psychological environment that does away with the threat of violent crime in this country and brings us to a position where police officers and guards can feel a sense of security and will not use their weapons for capital punishment without the due course of law.
I think we can underscore something that has been established over and over again. A negative kind of input or feed into society reflects itself with negative reactions. This has been done with children. It has been demonstrated psychologically that when people are fed negative kinds of information, the relationship of people one to another is usually that of a more violent negative society. It does not take a person with any academic understanding to quickly recognize that Canadian society today is compacted with negative input. The press hunts for the negative. We do not read the news in the papers, hear it over the radio or see it over television: all we get is a portion of the news, that which is negative.
Until there is a concerted effort in this country to emphasize some of the positive activities and relationships within our society, those who are of weakened psychological balance will always try to achieve public attention and recognition from others. Many actions of people are an attempt to gain recognition from their fellow man. If they cannot gain recognition in a positive sense, the struggle to be recognized is so great that they will gain it in a negative sense.
The obligation of government is not to do away with the position that has been long-standing within this country, but to create the kind of society that gives us a sense of peace and security. If they cannot do that, they have no right to bring forward a piece of legislation that attempts to enhance peace and security but undermines and erodes the opinions of Canadians generally that something is being done to offer a real feeling of security in this country.
It is of the utmost importance, I think, that members of parliament recognize that police officers and security guards are placed in a most vulnerable position should the bill pass unamended. We are placing what is the cornerstone of peace and security in this country, namely, our police forces who are in charge of enforcing the law, in extreme jeopardy. Those who write the law are putting those who enforce the law in an uncompromising position. What we owe these people is some symbol to show we support them. But we must do our work first by bringing about a greater degree of security in this country.
We can ruminate on this subject for some time, but as mentioned before in the House there has been much focus upon the architectural designs of our cities. For example, we can demonstrate statistically that if a city of 100,000 people expands to one of one million people, we should expand our police force sixtyfold, not tenfold. As we increase the size of our cities, so the rate of crime increases.
Studies of animals other than the human species have shown that crowding together produces a change in normal behavioural patterns. The Lithwick report on urbanization

in Canada discloses that in its founding year of 1867 about 80 per cent of the country was rural, whereas now is it something like 85 per cent urban. The report predicts that 95 per cent of all Canadians will be living in five cities by the year 2000.
Although we recognize the danger of concentrating masses of people within a small area, government policies fail to take account of this. I suggest that the transportation and communication policies of this country are winning out over social policies in terms of social welfare, law and order and simply the happiness of human living. We are bartering away what we call efficiency in communications and transportation so as to save money in one particular pocket, without recognizing that sooner or later we will have to pay the cost in another social sense. The fact of the matter is-

I simply want to add, Mr. Speaker, that it is not the size of cities that increases the crime rate in this country; it is also the architectural design of our cities. Some interesting studies have been made showing that apartment dwellers, especially those in certain designs of apartments, are a stimulus to the crime rate in this country. The very nature of housing and of housing policies in this country reflects the amount of crime that is committed, and as legislators I suggest we should have something more important to do than simply talk about whether we are retentionists or abolitionists.
This bill is removing from society one of the symbols of law and order. It will create a vacuum. I believe that all Canadians would quite willingly accept an abolitionist stance, but only after the government has demonstrated clearly that peace and security is the right of all Canadians, and that the government has put in place the right psychological environment from coast to coast, and from the forty-ninth to the pole, the kind of society in which violence is deterred.
This may sound in some ways as if we are being over optimistic about the role of government and the behaviour of people, but studies made in numerous countries of the world demonstrate that different societies do, in fact, have different rates of crime. Anyone observing the psychology of human behaviour soon recognizes that crime rates do not differ from one country to another simply because the respective populations live in two different countries but rather because the cultures are different. I suggest that Canadian society has got itself on the wrong track. In Canada violence has become entertainment, not only on television, in our movies and in the press, but even in sport and other activities. We enjoy violence.
In summary, what the amendment moved by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta is seeking is not a return to capital punishment per se, but is asking the Canadian people, through their members of parliament, whether or not the due process of law should be carried out. If we take away part of our present system of justice
July 7, 1976

and leave a vacuum in its place, one obvious result of this will be that the prison guards in this country will be more trigger-happy. They will have no other choice, since they will have been placed in a position of greater fear. This is why the legislation must be amended. Until we have earned the right to be truly an abolitionist state, this parliament has no right to take away what appears to be, to the policemen of this country, a sense of security. We must first assure our policemen-indeed, all Canadians- that it is safe to live in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I spoke on second reading of this bill and was not planning to speak on this motion. However, since my position is the complete opposite of that taken by the previous speaker I felt I should make a few comments.
I believe that the murder of a policeman or a prison guard is no more, or no less, important than the killing of a child, a fisherman or any other member of our society. I felt our present legislation was discriminatory in that it provided that only two classes in our society were of importance, in that only if a policeman or prison guard was murdered would capital punishment be carried out. I still feel that this is a discriminatory provision, and the sooner we get rid of the idea that some groups in society are more important than others, the better off we will be.
I believe in the retention of capital punishment, for a variety of reasons, but this is in relation to our whole Canadian society and not just one small part of it. The argument that a job is dangerous could be applied to any so-called dangerous job, such as that of a fireman, a pilot and of various other people in our society; but when they get into those jobs, they get into them with the realization that there are dangers involved. Having accepted those dangers, I do not think there should be further consideration given such as we have had under the legislation I consider to be improper, discriminatory and which in fact makes second-class citizens of those people who are not policemen or prison guards but who have been murdered over the years in Canada and in respect of which capital punishment was not applied. Many of us in this House have felt this way.
What are we now attempting to do? We have a motion before us that would attempt to bring back the same discriminatory practice that has existed and which many of us have decried for very good reason. I believe, in all honesty, that if we look at our society, not only in Canada but throughout the world, we will find that in the last 10, 12 or 14 years there has been a tremendous change and the change has occurred in respect of criminal activity. I think when you and I were growing up, Mr. Speaker, it would have required a very deep search to find a case of hijacking of an aircraft, of kidnapping or of terrorist activity. In order to be pragmatic, one would have to realize that our society has changed in the last 10 or 15 years. It is the duty of parliament to reflect these changes and to ensure that the law-abiding part of our society not only feels secure, but in fact is secure.
The argument in favour of capital punishment for premeditated murder is a very strong one. Anyone who becomes involved with premeditated murder for gain or
Capital Punishment
profit or as a result of organized crime should be dealt with quickly. I am afraid the milk of human kindness in my body runs very low for those people who go out on contract to kill another individual. Again, regardless of who that individual is, whether he be a policeman, a prison guard or just an ordinary citizen, I feel that person should be dealt with most severely. Such individuals must know that if they become involved in that sort of situation, the results will be dramatic, sudden and positive.
As I said earlier, I cannot vote for this particular motion and I trust that my colleagues who are retentionists cannot vote for it because it is discriminatory. It is a motion that would make second-class citizens of a great part of our population. Surely, this parliament must take actions which are non-discriminatory and should not allow a phrase or a principle like "second-class citizen" to occur in legislation. We are all equal in Canada, and the law should apply to all Canadians equally. I do not think we have an elite in society, and for that reason I will vote against this motion.

Mr. Speaker, the amendment of my colleague, seconded by the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence), would strike clause 4 from the bill in that it would introduce into our Criminal Code and our criminal law what is known popularly on television and elsewhere as "murder one" and "murder two". I thought we had escaped that horrible classification. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson) seems to take umbrage with the phrase "second-degree murder" in that it makes people second-class citizens. In any event, I could not catch the trend of his argument.
The result of my colleague's amendment would have the effect of maintaining in force section 214 of the Criminal Code. That was the section brought in at the time of the restricted interpretation of capital punishment, in 1967 I think it was. Prior to that, section 214, or its predecessor number, had regard to categories of capital murder and non-capital murder. There was a much wider application under section 214 because at that time it dealt with murder for gain, a killing committed as a result of another violent act such as armed robbery, rape, kidnapping and others, and in addition deliberate poisoning. Poisoning was capital murder for which the penalty was death. We are now back to define defining, again, categories of murder, but not capital murder. No, that would be treasonous, but treasonous in the linguistic sense.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Treason is out.

speechtext:
Yes, the word "treason" is out because it has an entirely different meaning within the context of this bill. Apparently it would be quite wrong to use "capital" and "non-capital" murder. Heaven preserve us from falling that low! I have been looking with considerable care through the evidence at the committee hearings and, with the greatest respect, there is very little discussion on this subject. Most of it seems to have involved parole. Let us look at some of the problems the courts will have to wrestle with in the future. We must remember that it is not what is said in this chamber, at the committee or by the minister, that will determine for the judges what shall be the interpretation of the statute. Let

July 7, 1976
Capital Punishment
us read what it says in clause 4. The new section of the Criminal Code will read as follows:
214. (1) Murder is first degree murder or second degree murder.
The new subsection (2) will read:
Murder is first degree murder when it is planned and deliberate.
I suggest to hon. members that the interpretation of the word "planned" will give the courts a good deal of exercise over the years. It is true that new subsection (3) gives one illustration of planned and deliberate murder, and that is the contract murder of one either in the underworld or by the hiring of a killer. That is the deliberate, planned killing of a person. But there still remain a great number of murders that are planned and deliberate. There is the individual who himself hunts and stalks another individual, regardless of the reason, and kills that person. The hunting is planned and the killing is deliberate whether it is accomplished with a gun, a knife, bare hands or a club. How long must the planning take place? I can plan something and do it deliberately within five minutes. That is not done on the spur of the moment; the spur of the moment is the instant reaction.
I recall a case in common law in Britain which caused trouble to the courts because of the definition that exists in respect of the charge of murder where there is no uncontrollable reaction in the individual. There is the example of the husband who discovered he was being cuckold and found another man in his wife's bed, and in a towering rage killed one or both of them. That has been classified as a legitimate defence to a charge of murder and the courts have so held up to the Court of Appeal. On the other hand we have the case of a husband who, being cuckold, lies in wait to spy on his wife and her paramour. They, having come to the home, he sits on a ladder up on the second storey window, looks in, sees the couple in bed, goes down the ladder, goes into the woodshed, gets an axe and then proceeds up the stairs to the room and kills one or both of the parties. This is an actual case, but I do not remember whether one or two persons were killed. That was deemed not to be justifiable homicide because it was not instantaneous. This man had planned to spy and in the event he discovered there was misconduct on the part of his wife and her paramour.

speechtext: What about the offence relating to a Peeping Tom?

speechtext:
It would hardly be in that category. The court held that was not a justifiable homicide. I suggest the courts would have just as difficult a time determining what is planned and deliberate. I expected the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) to participate in this debate. I invite the Solicitor General, or the Attorney General of Canada (Mr. Basford), to explain to the House what they mean by the words "planned and deliberate".
There is an example given in subsection 3 of section 214 of the contract murder. That is point number one. Now I shall look at first-degree murder, preserving, in effect, what now is contained in section 214 concerning a police officer, a police constable, and so on. I have always won-

dered about this, now that we are using private security firms for the maintenance of public peace.
I would want the Solicitor General to say that this includes personnel hired on a temporary basis by a security firm to keep the peace and public order, say at a football or hockey game or at a sale at a department store where security personnel are employed for the preservation and maintenance of the public peace, and are killed. Is it first-degree murder if an employee of a firm hired by the government of Canada to act as a night watchman in a government building is killed in the course of his duty? Those are questions which the law officers of the Crown must explain. It is not satisfactory that they sit, as I would say in French, muets comme une carpe, and expect anyone in the House to approve this legislation without explanation. I ask for that explanation as a lawyer who may be asked to interpret this section for the benefit of the public.
What is the intention of the government in this legislation? Are we to be treated, as we often are treated in the House, with deathless silence? I assure hon. members that I intend to put all these sections through an examination in order to see just what they mean.
In line 6 on page 4, subparagraph (b), we find the second category of individuals the killing of whom is deemed to be first-degree murder. This deals primarily with officials or security officers in a prison or jail. Why is there the designation of "permanent employee"? The person involved might be a temporary employee. He might be a university student who, in a temporary or casual capacity, is carrying out the duties of a security officer in a jail or prison. Such person is not a permanent employee. Is the killing of such a person to fall under subparagraph (c) which refers to a person working in a prison with the permission of the prison authorities and acting in the course of his work therein, or is subparagraph (c) merely to cover social workers and other persons?
Take the case of the hostage incident in New Westminster, for instance, where social workers going into the prison were with the prisoners, were taken hostage and one of them was killed. I would say that such a person, if employed by someone outside such as, say, the correctional service of the government of Canada or of any province, would be covered under subparagraph (c), but I am wondering about the "temporary" employee. I am being careful with the language. I trust we will have the word of the Solicitor General that he will participate in the debate on this clause. I ask for an explanation.

I know he is not listening. Next-and this was a point which was fully covered in debate yesterday-is the matter of piracy. The Solicitor General did not intervene in the debate to tell hon. members to refer to subclause 5(a) which reads:
Irrespective of whether a murder is planned and deliberate on the part of any person, murder is first degree murder in respect of a person when the death is caused by that person
(a) while committing or attempting to commit an offence under section 76.1 (hijacking aircraft)-
July 7, 1976

This is the answer to many of the questions that were put yesterday. It is first-degree murder if committed in the attempt of a hijacking and the killing does not have to be planned or deliberate, or in respect of a person when death is caused by that person-again, the consequential death of a plane hijacking or even kidnapping. Then we have first-degree murder, such as in the case in British Columbia where a man who was a convicted rapist has been charged with the murder of a young girl. I will go no further. He has not been tried and he has not admitted the offence. This is all I can say. But he would be charged with murder in the first degree. All murder that is not first-degree is second-degree. That, again, is what I would call legalistic jargon. We already have the provisions for hijacking of aircraft and the penalty therefor, kidnapping, rape, and so forth.
As I have said many times, I do not like section 214(1) as it stands in the Criminal Code. I much prefer the definition that existed prior to the 1967 amendments defining capital and non-capital murder. I do not like the amendment in clause 4 because it does away, by repealing section 214 of the Criminal Code, with the death penalty for murder, either first-degree or any other murder.
Therefore, I ask the House to accept the amendment of my colleague and to reject what I suggest is a very loosely-worded definition of murder in the first-degree when it is planned and deliberate, which is fraught with all sorts of danger in interpretation. I know that if it does become law it will cause difficulties in the courts.
I hold no brief for the particular advantage held by policemen, prison guards or security officers acting in the course of their duty. While their job is much harder, I do not think their lives are any more valuable than those of citizens walking on the streets. To that extent I am not in favour of the continuation of the principle of discrimination in favour of these individuals. In so saying, I do not want to detract in any way from the difficult job they are doing, the danger to which they are exposed and the far greater danger to which they will be exposed when, and if, Bill C-84 should come into force, because from then on it will cost a man nothing to slip a knife into the ribs of a security officer, to shoot a guard or to kill another prisoner, if he is in prison already.
You cannot get a life sentence on top of a life sentence. I suppose that if the individual was in prison for second-degree murder and was serving a short sentence, he could then be charged and convicted of first-degree murder. But then he could go merrily on his way. In my view, clause 4 of Bill C-84 compounds the difficulty. I do not like the present section, 214, but to me it would cause less difficulty than the proposed law. Therefore, I support the amendment of my colleague.
