Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments on these very important amendments. I had the opportunity like many others on second reading, to express the wish that Parliament defeat this piece of legislation and at the same time meet the wishes of a large number of Canadians. While respecting the opposing views expressed in this House, I urge all members to
Capital Punishment
consider the importance of our duty towards public opinion. I understand that many members listen to their own conscience, but I also wonder whether we should not take due consideration of the wishes of the majority of Canadians.
These amendments deal particularly with a second capital murder and ask that such a murder be considered as a first degree murder. This should not cause any problem to most members, and the amendment recommending that Parliament retain capital punishment for the murder of police officers and prison guards is a very serious and very important amendment. If we really want to protect society, we must consider this amendment very carefully, and I hope that some amendments for which I should like to commend the movers will be passed. It is unthinkable from the outset that all these amendments be rejected at one fell swoop.
The government introduced a piece of legislation; it has passed second reading and was finally reported from the committee. Some amendments are considered by the House, and their objective is to improve the legislation and to meet a need: public security. Given the circumstances, I dare believe that freedom of expression will make it possible to have some amendments passed.
As so many other hon. members, I should like very much to see the reaction of the government members to these amendments. To consolidate my argument on both amendments, I should like to quote from a letter. Perhaps it has been quoted in the House, but still I want to include it in my comments to remind the Solicitor General of the dangers inherent in going on supporting the bill he is advocating. The members of the Public Service Alliance of Canada sent us a letter. It was addressed to the Solicitor General, and at the same time to hon. members of the House, for their information, and I quote:
Before the final vote on Bill C-83, we want to ask you to consider, in your soul and conscience, the remarks made on June 15, 1976 by the Prime Minister of Canada in his speech in the House of Commons, as reported on page 14499 of Hansard: "I want to make it very clear that, if a majority of hon. members vote against abolition, some people are going to be hanged. Their death would be a direct consequence of the negative decision made by this House on this bill.
As for us, we appeal to your conscience and we take the opposite view of that expressed by Mr. Trudeau by saying that abolitionist would be responsible for all future murders of penitentiary employees and law enforcement officers, and we swear that each time one of these murders is committed, we shall impute them to all those who have supported the abolition of capital punishment.
Here are a few facts that you should consider in our opinion:
1-	The irresponsible attitude of penitentiary commissioners and directors before the pressure groups who visit the institutions;
2-	The lack of proper management by the authorities of most penal institutions in the country;
3-	The shocking convict classification system which endangers the life of penitentiary employees as well as the life of most convicts who only want to obey the rules they must follow during their prison term;
4-	The present lack of facilities likely to guarantee the protection and safety of the staff of the penal institutions and of the prisoners against these criminals who have nothing to lose because of the 25 years of imprisonment they would have to serve under Bill C-83.
For these reasons, the Hon. Warren Allmand, Solicitor General of Canada, who did not have the courage to reveal these facts to the members of the House of Commons, should, in all conscience, resign his ministerial responsibilities since he has lost the confidence of all penitentiary employees and all law enforcement officers in Canada.

July 7, 1976
Capital Punishment
It is still Mr. Caouette, the Secretary Treasurer of the Association who is speaking:
We urge you, in your heart of hearts, to consider the safety of your family and that of penitentiary employees and law enforcement officers while reflecting on these words: "We want everyone to clearly understand that if most members of Parliament vote against the retention of the death penalty, people will be murdered. The death of these people would then be a direct result of the negative decision made by the House of Commons on this bill."
Mr. Speaker, I believe that this letter is extremely important. That is an appeal made by those who are responsible for maintaining authority in our institutions. And I feel that those remarks should give us cause for serious reflection and prompt us into supporting the amendment we are advocating today.
I would believe that most members will understand the position in which those who are responsible for security in our institutions and in our country generally find themselves, and one only has to consider what has been going on those last few years to understand. As recently as a week ago, I think, a Montreal newspaper reported that a young Montreal police officer checking on an apartment in Montreal had been shot in the chest quite unhesitatingly. That is the kind of protection we get from this government.
They have introduced a piece of legislation which, far from giving us additional security, is of enormous concern to the population. Is there need to recall also, Mr. Speaker, that they do not dare hold a referendum to know what is the public opinion since they already know that Canadians would favour retention of capital punishment, bearing in mind the circumstances we are all aware of.
Besides, Mr. Speaker, I know that it is a question that has to be resolved deep in one's conscience and I respect everybody's position. I would like to be sure that the government members did not take that position merely to save the Solicitor General or the Prime Minister. I suggest that we have reasons to wonder, after all the comments and discussions we have had with various members of this House.
Once again, I am not assuming that anyone is dishonest. I believe the issue is important enough that no hon. member should take a decision concerning this legislation for the sole purpose of saving the Solicitor General's neck or defending government policy. I think I am right in asking that this issue be considered in the light of much more solid reasons than those I have just mentioned.
We are also often reminded of the following commandment: Thou shalt not kill. I have on hand some comments, some information given to me by a priest who is not reluctant to give his opinion and information to the members of this House, who were very happy to receive it. He says clearly:
While I am writing this, our members in the House of Commons are discussing the advisability of retaining or abolishing capital punishment ... What will be the situation when this article will be published?
I	would like to submit a few comments in favour of the retention of capital punishment.
I know different views were expressed from all sides. I think it is my responsibility to bring forward certain

arguments presented by someone who is, after all, a parish priest in Levis county. I quote:
(a) I point out that by "retention of capital punishment", I do not mean retention of hanging, but this: Anyone who criminally and voluntarily kills another person is liable to expiate his crime through the sacrifice of his own life if he is recognized as actually and legally responsible for this crime unless it has been committed by accident (manslaughter) or in case of self-defence.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that those remarks are perfectly related, at least to the group of people we wish to protect through the amendment before us. I continue:
(c) The retention of capital punishment is not a matter of revenge, but it is legal reparation of the most serious crime and is also aimed at protecting the life of the people in the interest of public weal and order.
Those are the reasons given by this parish priest for the retention of capital punishment:
1-	The inestimable price of life and its protection require the retention of capital punishment.
2-	The Holy Bible says in Genesis 9,6: "Who so sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed" and, in Exodus 21,23: "And if any mischief follow, then thou shalt give life for life".
3-	The Christian theology always recognized to the state the right to inflict capital punishment for instance in case of murder and this because of the invaluable price of life and for its protection and the protection of the whole society, this fair reparation is in the spirit of God and the Holy Bible.
4-	The Council of Trent says that the legitimate authority that condemns a murderer to death not only is not guilty of murder, but eminently obeys the fifth commandment that forbids murder.
5-	The Old Testament says in Exodus 21, 12: "He that smiteth a man, so that he die, shall be surely put to death".
I continue, Mr. Speaker, because I think that those comments should make us think. They might also relieve some consciences.
The Catholic Church always taught that the state has the right to apply capital punishment for a serious crime, like murder, and this to protect peace and security.
Christ himself said so to Pilate who told him: Do you not know that I have the authority to release you or crucify you? And Christ answered: You would have no authority over me if it was not given to you from above, that is to say by God. The state has the right to inflict capital punishment.
It was not a mere nobody who said this, Mr. Speaker.
6-	St. Tomas Aquinas teaches not only that is it permissible but that it is necessary to punish some criminals with death to protect society and for the good of all.
And the fear of a possible error concerning the real criminal is no reason to ignore thoses principles, no more so that an accidental error in an operation would justify the scrapping of that operation which might already have been very helpful... and would be later on.
In any event, one is condemned to death only when there are real proofs that he is in fact responsible for voluntary homocide.
I remember that the Solicitor General expressed his concern about the possibility of hanging an innocent, saying that the most destitute may not have the tools or the money required to defend themselves on an equal footing with the more wealthy. He recognized that often the poor do not have the same advantages or tools to defend themselves, and that the government had the responsibility of providing them with a perfect defence and all the tools required to face the better off. And I continue with the quotation:
How many times in the past have I heard someone say: "If it were not for the death penalty, I would do away with him".
Nowadays, we often hear: "I would not be afraid to kill because going to jail is not so bad, you get free food, free board; you only have to keep
July 7, 1976

quiet and eventually you are released, sometimes much sooner than expected-there is always the hope to get out... or to escape.
And if we look at what has happened over the last few years, we see that many indeed have managed to get out.
Therefore, a 25 years sentence or even life-imprisonment is not commensurate with the crime of murder.
I	am thinking of those old people cowardly murdered because of their alleged savings.
I am thinking of those children who were tortured and savagely killed by this second offender. The mother of one of those children is still in hospital and probably will be all her life, as she became mentally ill because of her insurmontable grief . . .
I have in mind the settling of scores between members of the underworld even they have a right to live.
Human lives are being taken away as easily as dog's . . . and then we feel pity for the criminal and we forget the innocent victim and the flight of his family as well as the protection of the public.
And I think it is a good thing to remind all those who point out regularly that we must respect life that we also have the basic duty of respecting the lives of innocent persons. I continue my quotation:
I now raise a specific point: what about the eternal destiny of the victim who, without expecting it, is thrown into eternity? .. . Was this person morally ready to appear before God? What will be the consequences?
In this view, the criminal condemned to death punishment will benefit, for he will at least have time to regret his sin and to get his soul ready for the judgment after paying with his life: this will be his last hope.
After all those considerations and being aware of how priceless life and its protection are . .. for the sake of peace and social security.. . knowing that murderers do commit second crimes. . . considering mainly the lack of proportion between the taking of a human life and the few years spent in prison in payment for such a crime, we can say that mercy and pardon are irrelevant and do not correspond to the importance of the situation.
And if we deny the courts any possibility of applying capital punishment when appropriate, we take a serious risk that people might do justice themselves. Consequences that might arise are already predictable.
Retaining capital punishment will not deter the state from trying to improve social conditions and our judicial system in order to prevent violent crime.
And there again, there is much to say and I think the state has a great deal to do in that direction.
. . . thus the state will consider this unexplainable tolerance which allows the mass media to spread violence, murders and immorality and condone crimes of passion where the killing of a man or a woman is seen an ordinary fact of life . . . Living conditions in prisons will also be changed to have prisoners work and improve on their behaviour instead of letting them get worse through idleness . . . and as society improves, murders will be prevented and capital punishment will no longer need to be applied while being maintained.
Canadians hope that their representatives will really take a position in terms of justice and of the well-being of the whole of our society.
I think it is most important that our courts should always be able to apply the death penalty when needed.
Besides, we should know that the individual that respects the lives of others will never have to fear or undergo capital punishment, even though it is maintained in the books.
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to make these few comments which, in my opinion, will make us ponder over that issue seriously, regardless of the opinions expressed so far by members of this House.
As a matter of fact, the amendment now under consideration is quite important and the law enforcement officers have already stated their views and their concern about it.
Capital Punishment
I hope that the members of this House will consider the amendment as absolutely essential, if we wish to attain the objective we call public security.
We do not hesitate to suggest to day that the bill now under consideration is inconsistent with the objective which the government is aiming at. The Solicitor General may say whatever he likes, his arguments have been knocked out by experts and people much more qualified than I am. I have personally observed certain facts in my own constituency.
They should shocked to learn that on second reading we endorsed that legislation by a small majority, hoping that the amendments would allow light to enter our conscience and we hope at least that the amendments will correct that legislation.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this amendment is particularly important. I hope that all members, no matter how they have approached this measure in the past, will give their support to the proposition before the House. We ask the law enforcement officers and the employees in our federal penitentiaries to accept a very special responsibility, one which weighs heavily upon them, and which should weigh heavily upon us as legislators because we know what they face in a society which has become increasingly violent. Somehow, we have to find a formula which will stamp out the escalation of violence which we see about us nationally and internationally.
I do not like quoting statistics to show what has happened to this country's murder rate, but undeniably it is going up. No one can convince me that the elimination of the death penalty will not result in the further increase of the number of people who in days ahead will die violently in this country.
When you stop to think of it, all members of this House, including the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford), the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand), the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the leader of my party (Mr. Clark), or anyone else believes in capital punishment. I say that for this reason: if any one of us faced the situation in which someone was either going to take our life or we had to kill to defend ourselves, there is no question in my mind what each and every one of us would decide. That being the case, each and every one of us believes in the ultimate punishment for an individual who has a determination to kill. Therefore, I cannot understand why some members would wish to oppose the strong demand of the public for parliament to mirror the public's feeling with regard to capital punishment.
The public has told us, in no uncertain terms, that it wants parliament to enact legislation which will make the death penalty the ultimate punishment for the ultimate crime. The amendment we are discussing does not go that far. It suggests that we should impose the ultimate punishment only on those who commit the ultimate crime against those charged with the special responsibilities of policing our nation and protecting us from the inmates incarcerated in our penal institutions. It says that only if the life of one
15138

July 7, 1976
Capital Punishment
of these persons is taken shall the criminal pay the supreme penalty.
I suggest, sir, that the general public which thinks parliament should be a mirror of public opinion and that parliamentarians ought not always to vote according to their personal convictions want the death penalty to be mandatory for a greater number of crimes than contemplated by this amendment. I am sure the general public supports the amendment we are discussing. Therefore, I suggest that if we adopt the amendment we shall let criminals know they face the supreme penalty if they kill certain individuals in our society. There should be no alteration of the present law. When such crimes take place, the criminals should pay the supreme penalty.
One hears many arguments about why we have capital punishment and why we should or should not have it. I hold in my hand a copy of a letter, which I gather was sent to all members of parliament, from Pastor Ernest Kennedy of the Forward Baptist Church, Cambridge, Ontario. The original letter was addressed to the pastor's member of parliament, the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman). It outlines why, in the pastor's view, capital punishment should be retained. I shall put on record some of the views expressed in the letter by the pastor of the Forward Baptist Church, because I am impressed by the sincerity of the man and by his interpretation of what the Bible says on capital punishment. The pastor's letter reads in part:
In all my reading concerning capital punishment, I have yet to find what I believe to be the basic reason for capital punishment. In the Book of Genesis, long before Abraham, Moses or the nation of Israel was in existence, God laid down a simple covenant with man, in Genesis 8:22 to 9:16. This convenant was to last "while the earth remaineth, for perpetual generations, and everlasting covenant." This covenant included:
1	Gen. 9:2-3: Man's dominion over the animals. Man is to kill animals for food and protection. Man is unique and given dominion over the animals.
2	Gen. 9:4: A commandment against cannibalism. Man is allowed to eat all kinds of vegetables and meats, but not human flesh which contains the life and living soul.
3	Gen. 9:5-6: Murder of another human being is forbidden, and capital punishment is to be enacted.
I note that the pastor used the authority of the Old Testament. Most of us realize that Christ used the Old Testament to assist in guiding his disciples during his lifetime, just as he has guided Christians ever since his crucifixion. Pastor Kennedy went on to say:
It is interesting here to notice the one and only reason given for capital punishment. Genesis 9:6, "Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man." The reasons for capital punishment is not vengeance, not to get even with the man, not an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth, not as a deterrent to others, not for the well-being of man or the protection of society, although some of these things in themselves may be true and involved. The reason God demands capital punishment is just the opposite reason the behavioural scientists want it stopped. God says man is not an animal, but is a created being, made in the image of God and the man who is murdered bears in some way, the image of God, his creator. Murder at its roots is rebellion against God who created and gave dignity to the man murdered.
Consider the following ways that man is the recipient of God's divine image and is, therefore, more than an animal.
1 Mentally-man has an intelligence, capacity to reason, to evaluate and criticize himself.

2	Morally-man has a conscience, a capacity to recognize moral values and make moral choices.
3	Socially-man has a society, a capacity to love and to be in personal, social relationships.
4	Creatively-man has dominion, a capacity to exercise his lordship over creation, to subdue the earth and to be creative.
5	Spiritually-man has a soul, a capacity to worship, to pray and to live in communion with God.
The man who puts a gun in his pocket and deliberately drives to the bank and shoots the teller is playing God. He is deciding that another human being should die and has chosen to destroy the image of God as created in the dignity of that man.
When a man is solemnly put to death by the government for deliberately and premeditately taking another man's life, it is in serious recognition to the nation that murder is not just another crime, but is the taking into one's hands the life of a human being who is created in the image of God.
The pastor concludes by saying:
Mr. Saltsman, in the light of what I have written, I trust that you will give serious consideration for the sake of our country, the responsibility of our government to God, and the dignity of human life to reverse your vote when the bill comes to third and final reading.
I believe that Mr. Kennedy has touched on the most significant aspect of this whole debate. It is not only to deter others from committing murder that we want capital punishment. We believe that when an individual commits a premeditated murder he is, in effect, playing God: he takes things into his own hands and destroys that life. By doing that, that individual sacrifices any hope of mercy by his fellow men. When he destroyed that individual, he destroyed a part of God. God himself said when that was done that individual sacrificed any right to live. That is the way it should be.
There is a penitentiary in my constituency, at Dorchester. There are a great many employees in my area who live and work in that maximum security institution. I have conversation on an almost constant basis with those employees. The kind of experimentation that has been imposed upon employees of penal institutions makes one shudder. There is a degree of permissiveness in our penal system today that gives little protection to the employees. It is no wonder that soon after the vote on second reading, when the bill was given approval in principle, a great many penitentiary employees in the province of Quebec resigned from their employment. If this government has no respect for their lives, they do. They knew that to continue their employment in those penitentiaries, without capital punishment on the statute books, was inviting the possibility of dying in their employment.
There must be a degree of protection for society in general and employees of penal institutions in particular. They must have a fair assurance that if they continue in their employment they will return home in the evening to their wives and families. However, that kind of assurance does not exist today. Therefore, I believe that capital punishment should be retained on the statute books. In fact, I believe it should be enforced in cases where individuals have been found guilty of capital murder and sentenced to death.
It is not a case of whether we are putting the noose around someone's neck, or someone else is: it is the law of the land. The courts of this land make a judgment with
July 7, 1976

regard to the penalty an individual should pay for a crime. Almost consistently since 1962 they have said that criminals who commit capital murder should die, especially in cases where the jury has not made a recommendation for mercy. However, that has not been the case.
At this time we have in our penitentiaries the most dangerous types of individuals, individuals who would not think twice of killing again. I think of Ambrose and Hutchison who were in Dorchester penitentiary. They showed no mercy. Indeed, they showed the most grotesque inhumanity in the murder of two police officers in Moncton. There is a great danger to every employee because of the inmates who are there. I think of the terrible penalty that inmates in penal institutions must pay so that the government can work out a public relations campaign to convince members of parliament to support abolition. The government says that inmates should remain in those institutions for a longer period of time. The government is trying to sell the public a hard line as far as individuals who have committed capital crimes are concerned.
I do not believe we are going down the right road as far as far as rehabilitation and reform of inmates in our penal institutions are concerned by taking a hard line and having longer sentences in order to eliminate the possibility of having to carry out the death penalty against a very small coterie of inmates who have committed capital murder-in other words, those who have killed a police officer or a penitentiary employee. I firmly believe that the citizens of this country would be quite willing to sacrifice the lives of the few who have been convicted and sentenced to death in order to develop a more realistic rehabilitation program within our penitentiary system.
I assume my time is running out. I will conclude by saying that I support this amendment, as I hope most hon. members will. If that is done, we will then be able to convince the Canadian public that we have acceptable protection for at least one segment of our society, those involved in law enforcement and the protection of society.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) for his intervention. He spoke of the Public Service Alliance of Canada. It was said that the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had claimed that those who were retentionists would be, in their soul and conscience, responsible for the death of the 11 criminals who are now waiting only for our decision to know whether they will live or hang.
I believe the individual who is about to commit a crime knows very well that, when he goes out to rob with a loaded firearm, if he shoots at a policeman he will obviously hit him and possibly kill him.
So all told there are now 11 criminals waiting to know if they will continue to live or not. Mr. Speaker, I try to be human with everybody; we know very well that the cabinet can commute these death penalties into life imprisonment penalties. On the other hand, if the House could retain capital punishment, particularly in the case of the murder of policemen and prison guards who are here to guarantee the security of society, then the would-be mur-
Capital Punishment
derers would know that if they commit crimes, there will be no mercy. Of course, we could argue that there are judicial errors, but today we know very well that people are not sentenced to death by hanging when there is the slightest doubt.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to be allowed to speak not only about the retention of capital punishment in the case of policemen and prison guards but also to say-and I wanted to take the floor again because I maintain my position- that if we want to reduce all this, we will be able to do it but only in the long term. And I quote from a document from the Public Service Alliance of Canada which all hon. members received and which is dated June 30, 1976. In the last paragraph of this brief, they say this: We asked the Solicitor General that his bill be tabled as long as he will not have provided for the establishment of a special institution responsible for the security, namely the safety and the security of all the employees of the Canadian penitentiary service who work in the institutions. We humbly ask you to do this on behalf of all the employees of penitentiaries and their families and so on.
Mr. Speaker, to prove to the House to just what extent the government puts forward a bill designed to abolish capital punishment, what is offered in return to society, what is offered to Canadian people to protect them? Nothing. As evidence, last October I asked the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Allmand) whether there was in his department anything planned to provide some grants to associations across the country, which would be used to curb juvenile delinquency and help reduce the crime rate.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, I want to explain to the House quite briefly, of course, why this bill is not justified, because they precisely forget to offer alternatives. The media can say that with or without capital punishment, nothing will change. Any one who wants to kill will kill anyway. I respect the opinion of my colleagues who feel that way. As far as I am concerned, I think that to provide the public with a minimum of protection, we must have maximum security in our penitentiary institutions, especially for those who guard the inmates. I am not saying you should give them all powers or extraordinary powers, no, but we must ensure the security of those convicts and maintain the death penalty for the murder of policemen who are there to protect us.
But can we afford, as legislators, to let this go, only to see people in our penal institutions strike or resign? A dozen or so have already done so. Can we afford it? In my view, no. Right now, I would like to go back to the prevention of juvenile delinquency and general crime, since, if we mean to prevent, we have to start somewhere. In my view we should start with youngsters aged 13 to 15. There was a patent discrepancy between the Solicitor General of Canada and his officials regarding programs to reduce the crime rate, starting from the basics.
Mr. Speaker, when some groups are interested in preventing crime in our society at the adult or youth level, I think the government ought to consider this solution while preserving the death penalty. And why maintain it? Simply because, as time marches on, within 5, 10 or 15 years, this prevention will be established and a new outlook will pervade our society. Instead of a violence prone society, we shall develop a new one which will encourage

people to produce for their country and to respect the rights of others.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, in today's society, we may have lost the sense of values, and this is why a host of young people hang around on street corners, sniff glue or what have you. We ask the government: What are you going to do to protect society against this kind of thing? How are you going to deal with the situation? They say: It is only a few. Of course, it may be so. They want to protect a minority.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: How true!

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
But what do we do as legislators as regards capital punishment? Actually, Mr. Speaker, in my heart of hearts, I am not the kind of man who would hang a criminal, but I believe that as a legislator, and after consulting my constituents, I must protect the majority of Canadians. This is my first concern.
Regardless of their views, be they abolitionists or reten-tionists, all members must act according to their own conscience. If abolitionists wish to vote according to their conscience, without consulting their constituents, they have the right to do so, and I respect it. I, for one, did the opposite and I will stick to my position in this regard.
Mr. Speaker, I said I would be brief. In conclusion, I wish to repeat what I said about prevention. Therefore, I will quote an extract of a booklet sent to us by the Solicitor General now and then and called "Liaison", a monthly publication on criminal justice, Volume I, issue 9, October 1975. The article is entitled "People and sentencing", and I quote.
I also have the feeling, like these school officials, that a wider use should be made of community services, open residential centres and other types of rehabilitation centres of a non-prison nature in which the young child, the juvenile delinquent and certainly the first-time offender would be looked after.
Mr. Speaker, all this comes down to say that today, when an individual is caught, even for the first time, he may have committed a crime using a gun or otherwise. Because even if he has committed a crime, this does not mean he is an habitual criminal. This one can be saved, I believe that, but when we make an habitual criminal of him, when we mix him with hardened criminals, at that point Parliament should have the opportunity to reexamine the whole penal system to ensure maximum security for prison guards and police officers and also to protect the population and some inmates who can be rehabilitated. We can give a chance to the criminals. That does not mean they should all be hanged.
Again last week, in Montreal, a man shot a policeman and fortunately the policeman was not killed. I am very glad for him but if the bullet had been deflected, maybe by a few inches, he would have been killed. Mr. Speaker, these people could not care less whether they kill a police officer or a prison guard. A man will be sent to prison for 25 or 35 years. What does he have to lose? He has nothing left to lose. For him, one crime more, one crime less, he is almost for life behind bars so he does not give a hoot, but we

should think of protecting those who try to protect society. That is why I support the motion. I agree, and I hope that the others, whatever their opinion, I respect it, may have the opportunity of reconsidering this motion and then, together, we can decide.
All I wish is that we finally provide this minimum of security to those whose duty is to protect us.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendment we have before us is in my opinion, very important. When we are discussing the protection of innocent citizens, when we are dealing with the importance of preventing criminals from continuing to play havoc with society, we are in fact speaking about the means to prevent criminals from going on killing innocent victims. When a criminal is sent to prison, no matter for how long, he is put into the hands of guards whose duties is to keep criminals away from society. In our opinion, this is, Mr. Speaker, protecting society.
Prison guards and police agents risk their lives protecting citizens against criminals. So honest citizens will not have to face hardened criminals those prison guards must live every day with people for whom human life has no value. Because of the bill which was introduced in the House they feel that the very same human life has no value in the eyes of the Solicitor General of Canada. Those policemen and prison guards risk their lives every day. At any moment they can see hardened criminals attack them to defend themselves since capital punishment will no longer exist for them.
They also risk everything they have to lose, those few years behind bars, everything they have, to allow other citizens to be protected against the actions of criminals. How does this government thank those valiant prison guards who risk their lives? Well, the only thank the Solicitor General gives them is the abolition of capital punishment, so that murderers sentenced to life have nothing to lose in escaping.
Mr. Speaker, when somebody has already been sentenced to life imprisonment what does he have to lose? We feel that he has absolutely nothing to lose by trying to escape if the maximum sentence he can get is life imprisonment, and we feel that sentence now exists. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, prison guards are at the mercy of the first inmate who decides to escape. Even if he were to kill a prison guard or two what is that going to change in his case? He is already sentenced to life imprisonment. At worst, he may be recaptured and sentenced once again to life imprisonment. Mr. Speaker, it is a bit like someone who has the mumps or the measles. Once you have had them, you cannot get them again. So, Mr. Speaker, the obvious consequence is that prison guards are no longer protected at all.
July 7, 1976

With the bill proposed by the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand), the lifer will be able to kill as many guards as he wishes as he will not get more than a life term. He has nothing to lose and everything to win by killing a guard in an escape attempt. If the Solicitor General himself was a prison guard and had to face those criminals every day, he would probably understand how important capital punishment is for those who must face criminals day in and day out.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, from his comfortable seat in the House of Commons it is easy for him to say that capital punishment is not useful and does not protect policemen and guards. If the Solicitor General had to cope with killers and criminals every day, as do policemen and guards, he would have a different view. He would not brag so much and would probably better understand the people responsible for maintaining peace and order who ask for the retention of capital punishment to have minimum protection against killers and criminals.
If the Solicitor General listens to policemen and prison guards, he will realize that they do not accept the attitude of the government and the personal attitude of the minister concerning that issue. I have here, Mr. Speaker, an article from the newspaper La Presse showing very clearly the intention of prison guards and policemen to join forces to fight the government bill. This is what the article says as it reflects the attitude of prison guards concerning the abolition of capital punishment.
Prison guards intend to join forces with policemen before going into action.
A new common front is about to appear. This time, it will be prison guards asking for the support of various Canadian police corps to give more weight to their demands.
That response came on the heels of the vote on second reading of the bill to abolish capital punishment. The security staff of the federal prisons in Quebec, gathered in a general meeting a few days ago, gave their union executives a mandate to rally all forces before using pressure tactics.
Many people in the audience were in favour of unlimited strike action. However, they accepted the idea of a common front so that the measures to be taken will have a real impact. Prison guards of several other Canadian cities also held meetings, a few days ago to protest against the government decision. Some prison guards said they would accept the abolition of capital punishment if super-maximum security jails are built, something that does not exist in Canada at this time.
"Criminals saved from the execution by the new legislation are a constant threat to our security" declared the guards at Saint-Vincent-de-Paul. "We cannot forget what happened to our colleague Paul Gosse-lin, killed last year by a prisoner".
Another guard who was held hostage a few weeks ago believes that he owes his life to the existence of the death penalty. "When I told my aggressor who was pointing a knife at me, if you kill me, you are liable to be hanged"...
And this guard sincerely believes that his aggressor thought twice and decided to leave him alive.
The executive of the prison guards union and top officials of the Public Service Alliance of Canada discussed a possible mutual agreement with policemen and obtained a clear mandate: we must strongly protest against abolition of the death penalty and negotiate once and for all for our security.
Capital Punishment
Mr. Speaker, I continue the quotation:
Mr. Jean-Guy Chalut, Vice-President of the Alliance for Quebec said he welcomes such a clear mandate and has assured guards that there would be new developments ...
-in the coming weeks.
According to Mr. Chalut, even the prisoners are against the abolition of the death penalty because they also fear for their life.
Mr. Speaker, when we read such comments, we wonder how a minister could come here to withdraw the only protection provided to those people, to assure some protection to every Canadian.
It is clear that prison guards fear for their life. Unlike the Solicitor General, they do not have the advantage of being constantly protected by the RCMP. They must live daily with people for whom human lives are worthless. Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock?
